h1: Where Can I See Oopbuy QC Photos?
metaDescription: Learn when Oopbuy QC photos become relevant, where to check for them, what to do if they are missing, and when to request extra angles.
searchIntent: Answer where Oopbuy QC photos fit before a shopper compares photos, product links, and size details.
quickAnswer: A public Oopbuy product-page interface reviewed for this guide showed QC photos becoming viewable after warehouse arrival. Start with the current item's order or warehouse details. The exact menu labels can change, so check the current interface and use Oopbuy support if the item is stocked but no photo area appears.
evidenceSummary: Searches around Oopbuy QC photos and QC finder pages show that shoppers want a clearer way to compare photos, links, and item details. Community posts and public page checks can show the question, but live Oopbuy pages should be checked for current paths and timing.

bodySections.heading: First, know which photos you are looking at
paragraphs: Three types of images can appear during product research. They serve different purposes, and mixing them up can lead to the wrong conclusion.

Seller or product-listing photos show how the seller presents the product before an order. They may use studio lighting, edited backgrounds, or selected angles. They do not show the specific item received for your order.

CuriCart product photos are research images connected to a CuriCart product record. They can help you compare visible details, SKU or size labels, listed price references, and marketplace source context before you inspect an item elsewhere. They are not Oopbuy warehouse-issued QC photos.
Oopbuy warehouse-issued QC photos relate to the warehouse stage. These are the images to look for when you want to inspect the specific received item shown in your warehouse or order record.
A polished listing photo is not evidence that the warehouse item looks the same. A research image also cannot replace the photo set attached to your Oopbuy warehouse item.

bodySections.heading: When QC photos normally become relevant
paragraphs: QC photos usually matter after the item has moved from source-page research into the warehouse stage. A public Oopbuy product-page interface reviewed for this guide showed a seller-to-warehouse sequence and connected quality inspection photos with warehouse arrival.

That supports one practical rule: check the item status before looking for QC photos. If the item has not reached the warehouse or has not been recorded as stocked, a warehouse photo set may not be ready or relevant yet.

The reviewed public page does not confirm a fixed upload time after warehouse receipt. It also does not establish one standard number of photos for every item. Treat timing, photo count, and interface labels as details to check on the current page.

bodySections.heading: How to locate Oopbuy QC photos without guessing the menu
paragraphs: Open the current item record in your logged-in Oopbuy account. Check the order details and the warehouse or stocked-item details available for that item. Look for a photo gallery, inspection area, or QC label connected to the same order record.
Interface labels can change. This guide does not give a fixed menu path that may be wrong for your account, device, or current Oopbuy layout.
Match the record carefully before reviewing any photos. The photo set only helps when it is attached to the same item, same order line, and same selected option you are checking.

If you cannot identify the correct photo area, contact Oopbuy through its current support channel. Include the order number and ask where the warehouse inspection images for that item appear in the current interface.

bodySections.heading: What to check if the photos are missing
paragraphs: Do not assume that a blank gallery means the photos were lost. A missing photo area can have several causes, and the right next step depends on the current item status.
bullets: Warehouse status: Confirm that the item has actually been recorded as received or stocked, not only shipped by the seller.
Correct item: Make sure you opened the right order line, especially when several similar products are in the account.
Correct image type: Seller-listing images are not the same as warehouse-issued QC photos.
Current page state: Reopen or refresh the item record and check the current web or app interface.
Support confirmation: If the item is stocked and the photo area is still absent, ask Oopbuy support to confirm the current status and location of the images.

bodySections.heading: When to request extra angles
paragraphs: A standard view may not show the detail that matters to you. An extra angle can be useful when the available images do not show a decision-critical area.
Describe one exact view instead of asking for more photos. For example, asking for the full inside label with readable text is clearer than asking for another picture.

A public Oopbuy interface reviewed for this guide showed custom-picture wording, but that does not prove every item has the same option, allowance, fee, or processing time. Check the current item interface before relying on extra-photo availability.
bullets: the inside of a hood, bag, or shoe;
a badge, print, or embroidery close-up;
the sole, heel, fastener, or hardware;
a visible measurement with the reference point clearly shown;
an area that appears covered, blurred, or outside the frame.

bodySections.heading: What QC photos can and cannot prove
paragraphs: QC photos can help you inspect visible details in the captured views. They are useful when the image is clear, the item record matches your order, and the detail you care about is actually visible.

You may be able to compare the overall item type, visible shape, selected color or style, readable size labels, seams, edges, prints, hardware, obvious marks, and whether an expected accessory is visibly present.

QC photos also have clear limits. They cannot prove authenticity, exact material composition, comfort, fit, long-term durability, hidden condition outside the photographed area, or exact color under different lighting and displays.
Use the photos as visual evidence, not as a guarantee. When a detail is too small, hidden, or blurred, the correct conclusion is not visible, not confirmed.

bodySections.heading: Research the product before warehouse QC exists
paragraphs: Warehouse-issued QC photos belong to a later stage than product discovery. Before that stage, you can still compare product category, source-page context, SKU or size notes, and visible product images.

Related product categories can help when you need more examples for visual comparison. Use them to compare photos, labels, size wording, option names, and source-page context. Do not treat a product-category example as Oopbuy warehouse QC evidence.

If a related product card or category helps you understand what to inspect next, open the live product or category page and confirm the visible information there. Product titles, option names, prices, and source-page details can change.

bodySections.heading: What to check before relying on it
paragraphs: Current Oopbuy screens can change, so check the live account page before treating any path or timing as final.

The exact account-menu path, standard photo count, free-photo allowance, extra-photo fee, processing time, and after-sales rules are not fixed by this guide. Check the current item interface or support response for those details.
Reddit questions and community replies are useful for seeing what shoppers struggle with. They should not be used as proof of current Oopbuy policy, pricing, service timing, or support rules.

bodySections.heading: What an Oopbuy QC Finder Means
paragraphs: People searching for an Oopbuy QC finder are usually not looking for another gallery. They want evidence that helps them judge a product before relying on a link or image set.

The word “finder” can describe different tools. One page may collect public product images. Another may match an item identifier with warehouse images. A spreadsheet may label a photo column as QC without explaining where the images came from. These pages do not provide the same evidence.
Start by identifying the photo type:
bullets: Seller listing photos show how a seller presents a product.
CuriCart product photos support product research and may sit beside SKU, size, style, listed-price, and source-link details.
Warehouse-issued QC photos document visible aspects of an item recorded at the warehouse stage.
Community images may come from another user, another order, or an unknown date.

bodySections.heading: Why People Search This
paragraphs: Searchers use terms such as “oopbuy qc finder,” “oopbuy qc photos,” and “oopbuy qc viewer” when they need more than a product thumbnail. They want to locate useful images, connect them to the correct item, and understand whether the result shows a listing photo, a warehouse image, or an image with no clear source.

Community discussions show the same practical problems. People ask where photos appear, why a result is missing, and how to find a more useful angle. The advice in those discussions can vary, so current menu labels, image options, charges, and timing still need to be confirmed on the live page.

A public Oopbuy product page has displayed photo-related labels including “QC Photos” and “Custom Pictures.” That makes it important to distinguish image areas instead of treating every photo result alike. Controls may differ by product, account, or current interface.

bodySections.heading: Step 1: Confirm the Item Reference
paragraphs: A finder result is only useful when you can connect it to a stable product reference.

Look for the original marketplace URL or a numeric item identifier. Preserve the complete link. Do not rely only on a product nickname, cropped screenshot, or spreadsheet row number. Generic names can point to several products, and sellers can use similar photos.

If the result shows an itemID, compare it character by character with the source record. A single different digit means you are reviewing a different record. If no itemID or source URL appears, treat the match as incomplete.

bodySections.heading: Step 2: Check Where the Images Came From
paragraphs: Look for a clear source label beside the images. The page should tell you whether the images are seller photos, warehouse photos, user submissions, or another type of reference.
Then check whether the page provides a date. An older image may still help you understand visible construction, but it cannot show the current state of a seller listing or a later item.
Avoid inferring image origin from the background alone. A neutral table, ruler, or warehouse-style backdrop may suggest an inspection setting, but appearance is not reliable provenance.

bodySections.heading: Step 3: Match the Product Option
paragraphs: The same source item can contain several colors, sizes, materials described by the seller, or style options. A finder result should identify the option shown.
Compare these visible records:
If the image set does not identify the selected option, it may still be useful for general visual research. It should not be treated as evidence for a specific variation.

Color or style label.
Size or SKU label.
Visible shape and design.
Accessories or packaging shown.

bodySections.heading: Step 4: Inspect Only What the Images Show
paragraphs: Use the images to answer narrow visual questions.

Possible observations include overall shape, color placement, printed text, visible stitching, hardware, sole pattern, label layout, or obvious marks. Zooming into a small file cannot create information that was never captured.
Write down the result as an observation:
Avoid conclusions such as “perfect quality” or “confirmed material.” Images cannot prove hidden construction, comfort, durability, exact composition, or authenticity.
bullets: “The heel area is outside the frame.”
“The left side shows a visible mark.”
“The color looks darker under this lighting.”

bodySections.heading: Step 5: Compare the Finder With the Source Page
paragraphs: Open the source record separately. Compare the title, itemID, listed price, options, and seller images with the finder result.

Differences are not automatically errors. The source page may have changed after the image was created. A finder may show another option. A spreadsheet may have shortened the title. Record each difference instead of forcing the pages to agree.
If the source page is unavailable, current option data and seller-page state remain unknown.

bodySections.heading: Step 6: Check Coverage Before Trusting Absence
paragraphs: A finder may not contain every product, every option, or every image set. An empty result does not prove that no QC photos exist.
Check whether the tool states its coverage, data source, and last update. If those details are absent, treat “no result” as “not found here.” Do not turn it into a platform-wide conclusion.

bodySections.heading: Common Mistakes
Treating every clean photo as QC
paragraphs: Studio photos and warehouse photos can both use plain backgrounds. Use source labels and item context, not visual style alone.

bodySections.heading: Ignoring the selected SKU
paragraphs: A photo of the correct model but the wrong color or size may answer only general design questions.

bodySections.heading: Assuming the newest result belongs to your item
paragraphs: A recent date does not connect an image to your order. Match the item identifier and option.

bodySections.heading: Using a finder as proof of platform policy
paragraphs: A third-party page cannot establish current Oopbuy menus, fees, photo rules, or service timing.

bodySections.heading: Treating “not found” as “does not exist”
paragraphs: Coverage may be partial. Check the current item record and source page before drawing a conclusion.

bodySections.heading: What Can Change
paragraphs: Finder coverage, source links, seller listings, product options, and page labels can change. A public result may be removed or replaced. A marketplace item may become unavailable. A third-party tool may stop updating without a clear notice.
Recheck the original source page on the day you make a decision. If the evidence matters to a specific warehouse item, use the current item record rather than an old public image set.
Current Oopbuy photo access rules, account paths, standard image counts, extra-image options, and charges were not established for this article. Confirm those details on the live Oopbuy interface.

bodySections.heading: What “With QC” Should Mean
paragraphs: The phrase “with QC” is often used loosely. It may mean that a spreadsheet links to warehouse-issued inspection photos. It may also mean that the row contains seller images, a public gallery, user-submitted photos, or a single thumbnail.
A spreadsheet should not use one label for all of these image types. The row needs enough context for a reader to understand what the image can support.

The most useful definition is evidence-based: a row marked with QC should identify where the images came from, what product and option they show, and when they were checked. If that context is missing, the row may still help discovery, but its QC claim is weak.

bodySections.heading: Why People Search This
paragraphs: Searchers looking for an “oopbuy spreadsheet with qc” usually want a faster way to compare products without losing the source record. Related searches focus on shoes, links, current lists, and photo context. The real need is not the largest sheet. It is a row that remains understandable and verifiable.

Community discussions also highlight mobile readability, clear categories, usable product records, and image references. Large inventory or frequent-update claims do not answer those needs unless individual rows show their source and check date.
Many spreadsheet pages provide attractive product grids but leave photo origin, row freshness, or source ownership unclear. A better spreadsheet makes those limitations visible.

bodySections.heading: Step 1: Require a Clear Product Identity
paragraphs: Every row should have a specific product title. A label such as “black shoes” is too broad. The title should help a user distinguish the model, visible style, and major option.

The row should also show a category. Use a simple category such as Shoe, Accessories, Electronics, Clothing, or Bags. A category helps users filter records and reduces mistaken comparisons between unrelated items.
If the spreadsheet uses an internal row ID, do not confuse it with the marketplace itemID. Both can appear, but their purpose should be labelled.

bodySections.heading: Step 2: Preserve the Original Source
paragraphs: A useful row retains the original marketplace URL. Short links, redirect pages, and copied titles are not substitutes for the source record.

For a Weidian item, the numeric itemID should be visible or recoverable from the original URL. If the spreadsheet links only to another tool, the user cannot easily confirm whether the destination still represents the same item.

The source link may stop working. That does not make the entire row useless, but the row should show a status such as checked, unavailable, changed, or unknown. It should also show the date of the last check.

bodySections.heading: Step 3: Label the Image Type
paragraphs: The spreadsheet should tell the reader what kind of image is displayed.
Recommended labels include:
Do not infer the label from the background. A ruler, neutral table, or plain wall does not prove warehouse provenance.
If a row links to several images, the label should apply to each group. Seller images and warehouse images should not be mixed in one gallery without separation.

bodySections.heading: Step 4: Show the Option Context
paragraphs: Photo comparison becomes more useful when the row records the option shown. Include visible SKU, color, size, or style text.
A single marketplace item may contain several variations. If the spreadsheet shows one photo but lists every available option, the reader needs to know which option the photo represents.
Use the seller’s visible wording when possible. Do not silently convert a short size label into another sizing system. If the row contains a conversion, name its source and date.

bodySections.heading: Step 5: Treat Price as a Reference
paragraphs: A spreadsheet can record a listed price observed on a source or research page. It should label that number as a reference and include a checked date.
The row should not present the number as a final cost. The visible source price can change, and it does not establish other platform amounts.
If a product has a price range, the spreadsheet should explain whether the range relates to different options. If that relationship is not visible, record the range without guessing.

bodySections.heading: Step 6: Record the Link and Image Check Date
paragraphs: “Updated” is not enough. A useful row includes an actual date for the source-link check and, when possible, a separate date for the image check.
These records help the reader understand age. They do not guarantee that the source remains unchanged after the check.
If a spreadsheet claims daily updates but provides no row-level dates or change log, the claim cannot be verified from the record.

bodySections.heading: Step 7: Mark Missing Details Clearly
paragraphs: An honest spreadsheet contains blank or Unknown fields when evidence is missing.
Fields that should stay marked as unknown include:
Unknown is more useful than an invented answer. It tells the reader what must be checked next.

bodySections.heading: Step 8: Check Mobile Usability
paragraphs: Many users open spreadsheet links on a phone. Important fields should remain readable without horizontal scanning across dozens of columns.
On mobile, place the core records first: product title, image, category, source link, option, photo type, and checked date. Secondary notes can expand below the row.
Buttons need descriptive text. “Open source” is clearer than an unlabeled icon. An image should have alt text that describes the product and photo type without making unsupported claims.

bodySections.heading: Common Mistakes
Ranking a spreadsheet by product count
paragraphs: A larger count does not prove current links, accurate labels, or useful images.

bodySections.heading: Calling every image QC
paragraphs: Seller photos and product-research photos can be valuable, but they need accurate labels.

bodySections.heading: Removing the original source URL
paragraphs: A row that routes through an unexplained destination is harder to verify.

bodySections.heading: Hiding stale links
paragraphs: Broken or changed links should remain visible as status information when the record has research value.

bodySections.heading: Treating reference price as a final amount
paragraphs: The spreadsheet should state where and when the visible price was observed.

bodySections.heading: Publishing duplicate rows
paragraphs: Two rows with the same itemID and different shortened names can mislead users into thinking they are separate products.

bodySections.heading: What Can Change
paragraphs: Marketplace pages, seller listings, product options, images, and prices can change. Spreadsheet maintainers can stop updating. A public photo page can disappear. An itemID may remain visible even when the source record is no longer available.
No spreadsheet can make a dynamic product record permanent. Its job is to preserve evidence and dates, not promise that every field remains current.
Current Oopbuy support for a particular source link, current platform rules, and any service terms must be checked on the live platform. A spreadsheet row cannot prove them.

paragraphs: Oopbuy's public Inspection Information page describes several warehouse actions. It says packages that meet receipt requirements are opened for a prohibited-item check, then weighed and stored. It also says the warehouse checks visible specifications such as quantity, color, and size.

The same page excludes issues such as color difference, size error, and usage effect from its inspection scope. A warehouse inspection record therefore does not confirm every visual, fit, or performance detail.
For troubleshooting, keep the stages separate:
The public page does not define how quickly every step finishes. Check the live item record instead of treating these events as simultaneous.
ordered: A carrier reports movement or delivery.
The warehouse receives the package.
The item is matched to the correct record.
The stated inspection and storage work is completed.
The item page exposes the related images or status.

bodySections.heading: Check the Photo Area for the Same SKU
paragraphs: When a photo section appears, compare it with the item details before judging the images. Confirm the product title, item identifier, selected color, selected size, and visible style notes.

Then count only the images attached to that record. Do not add seller listing photos, spreadsheet previews, or pictures from another product page to the warehouse set. They may help with comparison, but they come from a different source.

If the photo area is empty, record what you can see. Note whether the section itself is present, whether it shows a loading state, and whether any warning or issue label appears. A blank section, a missing section, and an item-level error are different observations.

bodySections.heading: Look for an Item-Level Issue
paragraphs: An image problem may be connected to the item record rather than the photo viewer. Check for a visible warning, unmatched option, incomplete specification, or source-page error.

A current public Oopbuy page for an unavailable record displays “Item not found” and says the item may be unavailable, the link may have expired, or the store may have closed. That message describes possible source-page states. It does not prove why a separate warehouse photo record is missing.
Keep the two questions apart:
A broken source link does not automatically erase an existing warehouse record. A working source link also does not prove that warehouse processing is complete.
bullets: Does the marketplace product link still resolve?
Does the warehouse item record show its own images and status?

bodySections.heading: Refresh the Record Without Losing Evidence
paragraphs: Save a screenshot with the item identifier, status, and check time. Reload the item page once, then record whether the state changed. Avoid switching among similar records during this check.

bodySections.heading: Prepare a Clear Support Record
paragraphs: If the item is shown in a warehouse stage but the expected images still do not appear, gather the smallest useful set of details:
Use the current help or support option shown on Oopbuy and ask about the specific item record. Do not share passwords, payment details, or unrelated account information publicly.
bullets: screenshot of the missing or empty image area;
time and device used for the check.

bodySections.heading: Product Photos and Warehouse QC Photos Are Different
paragraphs: Seller listing images present the product before warehouse handling. Spreadsheet images may come from listings, community posts, or warehouse records. CuriCart product pages provide photos and option context for early research. Oopbuy warehouse QC photos relate to an item after the relevant warehouse process.

Product photos can help identify expected color, panel layout, print position, or style. Warehouse images show the visible item attached to that record. Neither type proves hidden construction, fit, durability, or authenticity.

Before the warehouse stage, you can review product and source context through the CuriCart Oopbuy product-research topic. Keep that research separate from the warehouse images you are trying to locate.
For more detail on photo types, read where to find Oopbuy QC photos and what an Oopbuy QC finder can verify.

bodySections.heading: Common Mistakes
Treating carrier delivery as completed storage
paragraphs: Carrier tracking and warehouse status are different records. Check both.

bodySections.heading: Looking at the wrong item
paragraphs: Match the item identifier and selected option, not only the image.

bodySections.heading: Calling every product image a QC photo
paragraphs: Label seller, spreadsheet, CuriCart, and warehouse images by source.

bodySections.heading: Using another user's timing as a rule
paragraphs: A community report cannot establish the processing time for your item.

bodySections.heading: Contacting support without the current status
paragraphs: Include the item reference, exact status, and useful screenshots.

bodySections.heading: What This Check Cannot Confirm
paragraphs: This checklist cannot determine a fixed image-release time, a standard number of images, a fee for extra views, or the result of a support request. It also cannot confirm product quality, fit, hidden condition, seller reliability, or authenticity.

Those details either depend on the current Oopbuy account interface, the specific item, or information that is not available on the public pages reviewed for this guide. If the live page does not define a field, keep it unconfirmed.

bodySections.heading: Final Checklist
paragraphs: Before reporting that Oopbuy QC photos are not showing, confirm that you have:
bullets: matched the item or order reference;
separated carrier delivery from warehouse storage;
checked the photo area for the same SKU;
captured any warning or empty-state message;
refreshed once after saving the original state;
prepared screenshots without exposing private data;
used the current help or support path for that item.

faq.question: Why are there no Oopbuy QC photos when tracking says delivered?
faq.answer: The carrier's delivery event may not mean that warehouse intake, item matching, inspection, and storage are complete. Compare the carrier record with the exact status on the current Oopbuy item page.

faq.question: How long should Oopbuy QC photos take to appear?
faq.answer: The public pages reviewed for this guide do not establish one fixed time for every item. Check the current status and update time, then ask through the current support channel if the item appears stored but the image area remains incomplete.

faq.question: Are seller product photos the same as Oopbuy warehouse QC photos?
faq.answer: No. Seller photos belong to the marketplace listing. Warehouse QC photos relate to the item record after the relevant warehouse process. Keep their sources separate when comparing details.

faq.question: Should I request extra photos when the normal photo area is empty?
faq.answer: First confirm that the item record has reached the relevant warehouse stage and that the existing image section is actually missing or empty. Any current extra-photo option, price, allowance, or timing must be checked in the live Oopbuy interface.

faq.question: What should I include when asking about missing QC photos?
faq.answer: Include the item or order reference, exact status text, selected SKU, latest update time, and a screenshot of the photo area or warning. Do not post private account or payment information publicly.

title: How Should You Check an Oopbuy Spreadsheet for Shoes?
h1: How Should You Check an Oopbuy Spreadsheet for Shoes?
metaDescription: Check an Oopbuy shoe spreadsheet by comparing source links, itemID, product photos, style, size labels, price references, and update dates.
summary: Use a shoe spreadsheet checklist for model, source URL, itemID, image type, size labels, price references, and row freshness.
searchIntent: Show shoppers how to check shoe spreadsheet rows by source link, itemID, images, style, size, and price reference.
quickAnswer: Check an Oopbuy spreadsheet shoe row by matching the exact model, style, color, size system, product photos, listed-price reference, itemID, and original marketplace source. A useful row should make missing details visible instead of filling them with assumptions. Open the source page and compare every field before relying on the row. A spreadsheet can organize shoe research, but it cannot confirm current availability, fit, image origin, product condition, or Oopbuy handling by itself.
evidenceSummary: Use a shoe spreadsheet checklist for model, source URL, itemID, image type, size labels, price references, and row freshness.

bodySections.heading: Begin With a Complete Shoe Identity
paragraphs: A shoe name alone is not enough. One model can appear in several colors, materials, releases, or seller listings. A useful spreadsheet row should let you identify the exact version without depending on a small thumbnail.
Record these fields first:
If the row says only “white shoe,” “new runner,” or “best batch,” it does not provide a stable product identity. Promotional labels are not a replacement for the source title or item identifier.
Keep similar products separate. Two shoes may look alike while using different itemIDs, sizes, colors, or source pages.
bullets: brand or maker name as displayed;
style, version, or seller option label;
product type, such as running shoe, slide, or tennis shoe;

bodySections.heading: Open the Original Source Link
paragraphs: The source link is the row's most important verification path. It lets you compare the spreadsheet entry with the current marketplace record.

Check the destination domain and save the complete URL. For a Weidian page, look for the numeric itemID in the address. Compare that number with any itemID written in the spreadsheet. A mismatch means the two records need separate review.

Compare the visible title, seller context, images, price, and option labels. A working URL only shows that the page responded when checked. It does not confirm option availability or support elsewhere.
If the page fails, record the exact state and check date. An expired link, removed item, login screen, empty page, and identifier mismatch are different problems.
For a detailed source-record method, use the Oopbuy Weidian link guide.

bodySections.heading: Identify the Type of Every Image
paragraphs: An Oopbuy spreadsheet for shoes may show several kinds of images:

These images do not prove the same thing. A clean seller photo may help identify the intended style. A warehouse photo may show the visible item connected to a later record. A size-label photo may support one measurement comparison. None of them should be relabeled without a source.
A useful row should name the image type and source. If “QC” is not connected to an itemID, option, date, and warehouse record, call it a product photo or visual reference.
Use the Oopbuy spreadsheet-with-QC checklist when you need to evaluate image provenance and row completeness in more detail.

bodySections.heading: Read Size Labels Without Guessing
paragraphs: Shoe rows often combine EU, US, UK, CM, JP, men's, and women's labels. These labels must stay attached to the system shown on the source page.
Do not assume that a bare “42” means the same thing in every row. Do not treat a CM label as foot length unless the current chart defines it that way.
For each row, record:
If the spreadsheet and source page disagree, preserve both values and mark the difference.
The Oopbuy shoe size label guide explains how to keep labels, charts, foot measurements, and image measurements separate.
ordered: the exact size label;
the named size system;
whether the option is men's, women's, unisex, or undefined;
any centimetre measurement and what it measures;
the visible minimum and maximum options;
the source of any conversion.

bodySections.heading: Treat Price as a Dated Reference
paragraphs: A spreadsheet price is a dated reference. Record the currency, displayed amount, source, relevant option, and check date. A single number may not represent the current option or final amount.
If the row and source differ, keep the earlier value and record the new source state and date.

bodySections.heading: Check Row Freshness Field by Field
paragraphs: An “updated” badge is too broad. A strong shoe row shows when its key fields were checked.
Useful date fields include:
One current field does not make every field current. A working link may have a changed price or size range. If no check date appears, treat freshness as unknown.

bodySections.heading: Compare the Row With a Simple Worksheet
paragraphs: Use one line for the spreadsheet and one for the live source page. Then compare the fields side by side.
Use “Unknown” when the page does not define a field.
bullets: Field — Spreadsheet row — Current source page — Result
Complete model — Record exact wording — Record exact wording — Match / Different / Unknown
Style or color — Record visible option — Record current option — Match / Different / Unknown

bodySections.heading: Common Spreadsheet Mistakes
Ranking rows by popularity alone
paragraphs: Views or social mentions do not replace source, itemID, option, photo, price-date, and link checks.

bodySections.heading: Using one image to identify a shoe
paragraphs: Compare the title, style, itemID, options, and several visible angles.

bodySections.heading: Calling all images QC photos
paragraphs: Without clear warehouse provenance, use “product photo” or “visual reference.”

bodySections.heading: Converting sizes before reading the chart
paragraphs: Record the source label and measurement meaning before converting.

bodySections.heading: Treating the listed price as permanent
paragraphs: Keep currency, amount, source, and date together.

bodySections.heading: Hiding broken or changed links
paragraphs: Record the link state and what changed.

bodySections.heading: Shoe Row Checklist
paragraphs: Before relying on a row, confirm that it includes:
bullets: listed-price reference with currency and date;

bodySections.heading: What a Shoe Spreadsheet Cannot Prove
paragraphs: A spreadsheet cannot prove current availability, fit, comfort, hidden construction, durability, seller reliability, authenticity, or final price. It also cannot confirm whether Oopbuy currently accepts or handles a source link.
Use the spreadsheet to organize research. Use the current source page to verify the listing record. Keep later warehouse images and platform information as separate evidence.

faq.question: What should an Oopbuy spreadsheet shoe row include?
faq.answer: It should include the complete model, style or color, source URL, itemID, image type, size system, visible option range, listed-price reference, link state, and check date. Missing fields should be marked Unknown.

faq.question: Are spreadsheet shoe photos always QC photos?
faq.answer: No. They may be seller photos, product images, community photos, thumbnails, or warehouse-issued images. The row should identify the source before using the QC label.

faq.question: How do I check the size in an Oopbuy shoe spreadsheet?
faq.answer: Copy the exact option label and named size system. Compare it with the current source chart or option list. Do not guess what a bare number or centimetre value measures.

faq.question: Does a working source link mean the shoe is available?
faq.answer: No. It shows only that the page responded when checked. Confirm the current options and visible page state, and keep current availability unconfirmed unless the live record defines it.

faq.question: Can a spreadsheet tell me which shoe is the best choice?
faq.answer: It can organize product and source information. It cannot prove fit, quality, authenticity, seller reliability, or which option is right for you.
